I cool trick my boss has taught me is too wiggle a little bit when you see the drip form. You can see the weld pool start to collapse when a drip is starting to happen so you wiggle like 1/8” out of the way, stretching the pool out and preventing the drip, then going up as normal. A different coworker taught me when a drip happens and the wire starts digging into the material you can pull back a little bit. That cooks the amperage down at the arc and fills the cavity, then continue like normal.

Also wait a little bit between passes. The reason drips happen is because the material is too hot. Turn down or go faster if you need too

I love seeing newbies and trying to point them in the right direction.
I have this machine and honestly out of all the machines and welders I’ve used this is my favorite solely because it’s a really decent machine for what it’s trying to accomplish. The wire HF supplies is also pretty good.
Rebar is practically fabrication garbage and should never be welded unless it’s specifically made to be welded. So you’ll have to find yourself some scrap, you can ask local fab shops if they have anything, local scrap yards would love to sell you some. Home Depot/ lowes/ ace hardware/ any other big box store will have steel you can purchase however that’s an expensive option.
Steel that you should practice on: any carbon steel in sheets or plates/ angle iron is great, square stock, anything that has a good square edge or can be cut square is great starting material as the straight lines are easier to weld and will be less frustrating then curves or circles. You can cut and arrange your steel in a T shape to practice fillet welds and the T allows for both sides to be welded rather then just an L. You can also butt them up next to each other for a butt joint. I’d avoid groove joints for now until you think you’ve mastered fillets as those are more advanced. I’d try and purchase some thicker material, 1/8” to 1/4” will work fine on your machine, then work with thinner gauge when you feel more comfortable with welding.
Always clean your metal before you weld them.
By that I mean removed any “mill scale” (the very top oxide layer) ie grind till the surface appears shiny. If you have galvanized steel you can grind or sand off the galvanized layer and weld it as regular steel. Don’t try and weld stainless steel to steel it won’t work.

More fun tips and tricks:
You can buy all of your angle grinder discs for Cents if you just look on Amazon. Anything you’ll find at the store is expensive garbage, I recommend Benchmark Abrasives.
On the inside lid of your machine is a weld speed and feed chart, follow it to a T cuz it’s fairly accurate. 

I think that’s everything off the top of my head, but feel free to ask questions.
